title: What Charles Leclerc 'didn't understand' about Ferrari's Zandvoort F1 strategy
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc questioned a Ferrari strategy decision during the Dutch Grand Prix that potentially cost him a podium finish at Zandvoort. The call in question was his pitstop at the end of lap 43, which left the Monegasque with no real weapons to battle George Russell for third in the closing stages of the Formula 1 race. “I didn't really understand why we had to box so close to George's pitstop,” Leclerc said after the race, speaking to Sky Sports. “Because that really was kind of signing to finishing behind George, because with a two or three laps difference, for me there wasn't much I could have done, and I felt like there was a bit more in my tyres.” Leclerc was within a second of Russell before the Mercedes driver dived into the pitlane at the end of lap 40 - and could potentially have extended his stint to try to create enough of an offset in tyre life compared to his rival. That tactic proved successful in the race, as this was exactly the strategy that allowed Lando Norris to win. After being stuck behind Kimi Antonelli for almost the entire race, the McLaren driver made his last stop seven laps later than the Italian - and then quickly closed the gap and overtook the Mercedes for the lead. Ferrari, instead, pitted Leclerc just three laps after Russell. Speaking to the media after the race, the Monegasque driver said he felt that by doing so he was effectively throwing in the towel in the battle with the Mercedes. “I was very surprised to box so early when we had done exactly what we wanted,” he said. “George was pitting and so that was the time for us to do five, ten laps longer to build a tyre delta and to come back at the end on George. “Unfortunately, two laps later I was told to box, which I did I think three laps later.”

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

One contributing factor to Ferrari asking Leclerc to box earlier than he wanted was, perhaps, Lewis Hamilton. Being on a different strategy, the seven-time world champion caught up with Leclerc right at a crucial moment in his race - and demanded that the team swap the cars around. Whether the team decided to call Leclerc in to avoid slowing Hamilton down is unclear - but Leclerc confirmed he wanted to stay out. Read Also:

Formula 1What Ferrari actually meant to do when Lewis Hamilton felt like a "guinea pig"

Formula 1Lewis Hamilton explains Dutch GP radio outburst over team orders

“I need to review the way the situation was looking,” he said, when asked whether he’d been willing to swap positions with Hamilton and extend his stint, “but I was happy to go longer.” The initial call from Ferrari to box came on lap 42, but Leclerc responded to his engineer with a question: “What do you mean? This fucks my race if I stop two laps after Russell.” Having heard nothing in response, Leclerc added a few seconds later: “Hello?”. “Yeah coming back to you”, replied his engineer and then later confirmed: “Charles, we want to box” - but the driver drove past the pitlane entry, seemingly still disagreeing with the call - only to hear the command again to pit on the next lap: “So box Charles box, will be for hard.” After his stop, he emerged from the pits with a gap to Russell of around six seconds - and closed it down to less than two seconds a dozen laps later. Still, the pace difference was too small to count on an overtake on track, as Zandvoort requires a bigger delta. At that point, he could still have been in contention for a fourth-place finish, as Ferrari left Hamilton on track trying to extend his stint to the end of the race, but given the pace difference, the Briton would likely still have fallen behind both Russell and Leclerc. Yet the VSC on lap 55 offered Ferrari an opportunity to box Hamilton - which the team used. Leclerc pitted too, which locked him into fifth. He caught up with his team-mate, who was chasing Russell at the very end of the race, but both Ferrari drivers ultimately finished behind the Mercedes.

Undercut opportunity missed The race proved to be one in which Ferrari couldn’t capitalise on its very strong pace due to several factors. Leclerc’s race could have unfolded very differently had he not lost the position to Oscar Piastri at the restart. But stuck behind the Australian during his first stint, Leclerc couldn’t use his Ferrari’s pace to challenge the leaders.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

The team delayed his first stop and then opted for the medium compound - compared to Piastri’s hard - to help him get past the McLaren driver, but a slow stop meant he exited the pits six seconds behind the Australian. It took Leclerc only six laps to close in on Piastri and he eventually passed him on lap 34. By that time Russell was only three seconds up the road - and Leclerc closed that gap just in time for Ferrari to try to undercut the Mercedes. As Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur revealed after the race, that was the initial plan, but the Scuderia strategists hesitated. “I think it's a lot about execution,” admitted Vasseur, speaking to Sky Germany. “Pace was good and even strong, I think, compared to Mercedes. The issue is that at the second start we lost position on Piastri. We were stuck behind him. We lost a lot of time - and then when we were able to be in front, at one stage we were quite close to the undercut on Russell. But there was a group of cars, a bit of confusion - and we didn't do it. “It's our mistake, my mistake. But overall it's more a matter of execution.” At the end of lap 40, Ferrari told Leclerc, “Box opposite to Russell”, but as the Mercedes driver came in, the undercut opportunity was gone. Despite Vasseur saying it was a mistake not to box Leclerc a lap earlier, that might not have worked either, as Charles would have emerged on track right behind a group of lapped cars comprising Carlos Sainz, Franco Colapinto and Arvid Lindblad - and they could have prevented him from fully exploiting the opportunity on the outlap. After that, the only real chance for Leclerc to fight for third was to delay his second stop and try to create enough of a tyre delta compared to Russell - but Ferrari ultimately didn’t use it. As a result, despite Vasseur saying Ferrari’s pace was stronger on Sunday than Mercedes’, it was Antonelli and Russell who finished on the podium, with Hamilton and Leclerc right behind.

Frederic Vasseur, Ferrari Photo by: Bryn Lennon / Formula 1 via Getty Images

As the Monegasque pointed out after the race, despite Ferrari probably not maximising its strategy, the biggest issue for the Scuderia at Zandvoort was that it couldn’t use its race pace on Sunday, mainly because of its lowly grid positions - as the team struggled to match its rivals in qualifying. With Hamilton and Leclerc ending up on the third row at a track where overtaking is difficult, Ferrari was left trying to beat its rivals with strategy. “I mean a frustrating race to be honest,” Leclerc said after the finish, “because things went the wrong way for things we cannot really control, with the virtual safety car timing, it wasn't so great for us. But at the end of the day I think the pace was strong, we had a good overtake on Oscar, I think good tyre management. “The thing we need to understand is our qualifying pace. This is truly where we are lacking at the moment.” Read Also:

title: Lewis Hamilton apologises for Ferrari radio fury: "That wasn’t the best version of me"
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton says his Dutch Grand Prix frustration "wasn’t the best version of me" as he apologised to his Ferrari Formula 1 team for his frustration boiling over on team radio. During the second half of the race, Hamilton grew increasingly frustrated at the lack of strategy updates from Ferrari, especially once he got stuck behind team-mate Charles Leclerc, who was slower than the Briton on older tyres. “Great way of wasting time guys, good job,” a sarcastic Hamilton fired over on the airwaves once Leclerc finally pitted on lap 43. After the race, Hamilton said Ferrari still had steps to make on race weekend execution, pointing to Mercedes' much slicker swap between George Russell and Kimi Antonelli as a source of inspiration. But for Ferrari, the picture was a little bit more complicated than that, as the team was planning to pit Leclerc earlier but had to extend his stint for another lap to avoid traffic. At the same time, the plan for Hamilton was to stay on track until the end of the race, but team principal Vasseur explained Ferrari didn't want to alert its rivals to its strategy, so it decided not to communicate it straight away. Taking to social media, Hamilton has now apologised to his team for his heated radio exchanges, admitting it "wasn’t the best version of me".

"I’ve listened back to some of my radio and TV comments. In the heat of the moment frustration can come out, especially when you care as deeply as I do," Hamilton wrote. "But that wasn’t the best version of me. I take responsibility for that, and I’ll be better. "That passion comes from believing in this team, the people in it, and what we’re building together. The direction is clear. The belief is there. And the fight is absolutely still on."

Charles Leclerc leading Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Hamilton was buoyed by Ferrari's recent progress as its relentless car upgrade programme has allowed both him and team-mate Leclerc to win a grand prix, with Hamilton holding third in the drivers' championship on equal points with second-placed Russell. "I’m incredibly proud of everyone back at the factory who continues to bring updates, find performance and push us forward," the seven-time world champion added. "To the team at the track, thank you. The commitment and effort never go unnoticed. We still have work to do, particularly over one lap, but we’ll keep digging in, learning and improving together." title: McLaren appealing Monaco GP result "with a double intent"
excerpt:
McLaren Formula 1 team principal Andrea Stella says its appeal against the Monaco Grand Prix result, which is being held on Tuesday, stems from its concern for "the integrity of the sport". On Tuesday, the FIA's International Court of Appeal is handling an appeal by McLaren and Red Bull against the result of June's Monaco Grand Prix, in which several drivers were handed time penalties for exceeding pitlane speed limits, including McLaren's Oscar Piastri and Alpine driver Pierre Gasly. Afterwards, it emerged those pitlane infractions were false flags, caused by a timing loop error at the start of Monaco's unique pit entry. All drivers, other than Gasly (and his Alpine team-mate Franco Colapinto), had already served their time penalties during the race, while the Frenchman was handed a double five-second time penalty at the flag, demoting him from third to seventh. After Alpine launched a Right of Review against Gasly's penalties, the stewards rescinded both and restored the Frenchman's podium berth, which demoted Red Bull's Isack Hadjar to fourth and also bumped Piastri down the order. As a result, both McLaren and Red Bull launched an appeal procedure, because they took issue with Gasly's penalty being rescinded while other drivers, including Piastri, had no such opportunity. Anticipating the hearing, which takes place across Tuesday but could potentially drag on for longer, McLaren boss Stella said the team was both looking after its own interest in the constructors' standings and the interest of the series in general.

Monaco 2026 podium Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

"We go to the hearing at the International Court of Appeal with a double intent," Stella said on Sunday after the Dutch Grand Prix. "The first intent is more general than the interest of McLaren. "We think that the process that happened after the race in Monaco needs to be reviewed because from fairness for all competitors, the fact that the penalty was removed introduces some significant elements of concern. And we would like to take the opportunity of the International Court of Appeal for a clarification of this aspect. "There's obviously more related to this case. It can go into the technical aspects of how the pit limiter speed was calculated. But for me, at a high level, it's more the fairness and the principle that needs to be clarified and possibly reinstated." He added: "The second aspect is the interest of McLaren ourselves. We were also materially penalised for having served a penalty that is not appealable and this cost us points in the championship. "So, there's a general interest for Formula 1 and the integrity of the sport. And there's a material interest for McLaren in terms of our championship impact. These are the two points of view, the two perspectives that we would like to pursue and seek clarification for in the coming International Court of Appeal." Read Also:

title: Max Verstappen to face 100 drivers in ‘world’s biggest kart race’
excerpt:
Formula 1 star Max Verstappen will take on a new challenge next month when he goes up against 100 drivers in what has been touted as the world’s biggest kart race. The Red Bull driver will line up on the back of the grid at a purpose-built kart layout at Silverstone on 16 September, and be tasked with overtaking all 100 rivals before the time runs out. The race, named ‘Max vs 100’ will be broadcast live on Disney+ around the globe and ESPN in the US. The Dutchman will be up against a field comprising stars from various disciplines, including Red Bull athletes, celebrities, content creators and everyday fans. While the full entry list is yet to be released, Red Bull has already confirmed the participation of ultrarunner Arda Saatçi, basketball star Chris Matthews, freestyle mountain biker Matt Jones and streamers TheGrefg, Caedrel and TheDonato. Verstappen, who started his own career in karting at the age of four before rising through the ranks to make his F1 debut with Toro Rosso (now Racing Bulls) at the age of 17, said: “In go-karts you learn all the basics: starts, defending, overtaking. “Of course, I spent a long period of my life go-karting, so it's always nice to return. It’s about understanding the grip of the go-kart. I've done so many years in go-karting that you quite naturally get back into things."

In a statement, Red Bull said the broadcast will use game-inspired graphics and cinematic drone footage. Further, Verstappen will be able to talk directly to his rivals using radio, in stark contrast to F1 races where drivers can only communicate with their respective teams or the race control. French driver and race director David Terrien has designed the layout for the kart race at Silverstone, with Terrien himself testing it out with two-time iRacing World Champion Sebastian Job. “When you have Max Verstappen chasing everyone, I think that's going to be the experience of a lifetime for all the drivers,” Terrien said. “You're going to have Max showcasing all these skills of looking through the traffic, trying to prepare and plan where he can overtake people, and going through the traffic at the fastest speed he can because he doesn't want to let the drivers at the front pull away.” Job added: "I think to overtake 100 cars is going to be extremely difficult. Today we did it with 50, and even that was a challenge to do it in the allotted time. He's got his work cut out for him big time." Read Also:

title: FIA condemns online abuse at F1 stewards following Colapinto's Dutch GP penalty
excerpt:
Formula 1's governing body the FIA condemned the online harassment directed at its race stewards following their decision to apply the rulebook and penalise Alpine driver Franco Colapinto at Zandvoort. Colapinto and Racing Bulls rookie Arvid Lindblad were both handed drive-through penalties for overtaking under a double-waved yellow flag on lap one of the race. At the end of the lap, the yellows came out for a big crash involving Red Bull's Max Verstappen, which neutralised the final marshal sector until the start-finish straight. The first half of lap two was green again until race control decided to throw a red flag. As the yellows came out, Colapinto completed an overtake on Racing Bulls driver Yuki Tsunoda coming out of Zandvoort's final corner, while Lindblad drafted past Alpine's Pierre Gasly before crossing the start-finish line, after both drivers had been forced to take evasive action for debris. Referring to the Colapinto incident, the FIA stewards wrote: "Car 43 was behind Car 22 entering Turn 14 and overtook Car 22 in the double yellow flag sector before the line at the end of Lap 1. "Normally, such infringement requires a 10-second stop-go penalty, but the Stewards acknowledge the complications caused by the significant amount of debris on track at this point and take this into account as mitigating circumstances." The stewards also offered an identically phrased verdict for Lindblad.

Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Colapinto felt his penalty was "extremely harsh" as he overtook Tsunoda a split second after the yellows came out. However, according to the letter of the rulebook both drivers' penalties were clear-cut cases as the governing body takes safety related infractions particularly seriously. Colapinto's Argentinian sponsor Mercado Libre went much further on social media, questioning the FIA stewards' integrity. "The Stewards are killing the integrity of F1. This season they are proving to be horrible and impacting race results," said Mercado Libre's chief marketing officer Sean Summers, who has since removed the post. "Incompetence? Dishonesty? Both? Something is seriously broken in that organisation's culture." The sponsor's inflammatory comments further stoked the flames on social media as the FIA stewards received abusive threats, while Alpine's own social accounts were also targeted because a vocal subset of Argentinian fans felt the team did not back Colapinto enough in the case.

On Monday, Alpine stated: "We fully trust the FIA and the stewards when it comes to the policing of these rules and the application of sporting penalties during a live race scenario. "We believe the penalties applied for yellow flag Infringements during the opening laps of the Dutch Grand Prix were indeed harsh, but acknowledge they fit the punishment based on the letter of the law and were consistently applied across all competitors and is something we can review and learn from as a team."

Franco Colapinto, Alpine Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

The FIA, which has established the United Against Online Abuse campaign to tackle online abuse in sport, is understood to be exploring legal options and has released the following statement. "Following the Dutch Grand Prix, FIA stewards were targeted with online abuse after applying sporting penalties in line with FIA regulations," a statement read. "The United Against Online Abuse Coalition condemns all forms of abuse and harassment. Disagreement with decisions is part of sport, but it must never justify threats or personal attacks. "In 2023, the FIA launched the United Against Online Abuse Coalition after a steward faced targeted abuse following the United States Grand Prix. We urge everyone engaging with our sport to do so with respect and responsibility, online and offline." Among the toxic abuse hurled at the FIA, it was suggested Colapinto was penalised because of his nationality, with there being perceived bias against non-British drivers. Lindblad, who was given an identical penalty for a very similar infraction, is British. Read Also:

title: George Russell: “Specialist” Lando Norris always strong at tracks like Zandvoort
excerpt:
George Russell says Lando Norris has “always been a bit of a specialist” at circuits with long corners and high tyre degradation, so he wasn’t surprised to see the McLaren Formula 1 driver take back-to-back wins in Hungary and the Netherlands. Reigning F1 world champion Norris has taken pole and victory at both the Hungaroring and Zandvoort either side of the summer break – a development coupled up with a significant McLaren upgrade package. However, Russell pointed to Norris as a driver who has always shown strong performances at tracks like the Hungaroring and Zandvoort, given their similar characteristics with long corners and high tyre degradation. “I don’t think it’s a major surprise for us, seeing how competitive Lando was this weekend, considering he won in Budapest,” Russell said after finishing third in the Dutch Grand Prix. “It’s a very similar circuit with the long corners, high tyre degradation, with the two-stop strategy, so there’s a lot of similarities between the two circuits. I think this may continue for the coming two or three races until we start to bring more to the car, and fingers crossed our competitors don’t.” Next up is Monza that, while it does have a couple of long corners, is predominantly a circuit characterised by long straights, heavy braking zones and low-speed chicanes.

Lando Norris, McLaren, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

While F1’s engine battery and energy harvesting issue is likely to be exposed to its greatest limit at Monza and dominate conversation, Russell expects Mercedes to perform better at the Italian track given the team’s good showing at the likes of Shanghai, Montreal and Silverstone so far this year. “I think we will be slightly more competitive there,” Russell said of Monza. “However, I believe Ferrari have an engine upgrade incoming, and the truth is we just don’t know. “But I do believe that these high-degradation circuits really suit McLaren very well, and especially Lando. He’s always been a bit of a specialist in those conditions. We also saw it last year. “Monza may be slightly different, but I think they are the team to beat right now.” Russell’s team-mate Kimi Antonelli is set to serve a back-of-the-grid penalty at his home round in Monza for a full Mercedes power unit change which takes him out of his allocation. title: Max Verstappen was "lucky" to avoid Dutch GP pile-up, says Nico Rosberg
excerpt:
2016 Formula 1 champion Nico Rosberg argued that Red Bull driver Max Verstappen was lucky to avoid triggering a multi-car pile-up during his opening-lap crash at the Dutch Grand Prix. The four-time champion suffered a violent crash on the first lap of his home grand prix in damp conditions, which triggered the red flag and ended his race early. Luckily, no other driver was caught up in the crash, although Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto spun behind Verstappen in an unrelated incident and managed to continue. Speaking on Sky Sports F1 following the race, Rosberg explained: "Everybody's here cheering him on and then to go out of the race so early on like that, but it was the conditions. "It's just so incredibly hard in those conditions and especially on the slick tyre to judge the limit of the grip there, and so even the greatest of the moment, the greatest driver here, had a big crash. "And as Max said, we really got lucky there because if he spins and remains in the middle of the track and you have the whole pack coming at full speed, that could be a multi-car massive shunt with people driving right into him. That could have been a really bad outcome, so he even got a bit lucky there." As a result of the crash, Verstappen walked away from his home race weekend with just three points, which he collected from a sixth-place finish in the sprint race. The Dutchman currently sits sixth in the drivers' standings with 112 points, 130 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

While speaking to Sky Sports F1 after his early exit from the race, Verstappen confirmed that he is looking to maximise everything he can from the car but that, realistically, he is in the fourth-fastest car on the grid. "I mean, if you look at the average, the whole season we have been fourth fastest," he said. "So, I think this weekend really highlighted that, so we're definitely a little bit behind. We want to be closer. Maybe Monza we are, but I don't know. "We're getting towards the end of the season. You also have to look at next year. I think there are a few things in the car that we are looking at that can only be changed next year to really find a lot more performance. "So, we will just try to maximise everything we can with this car. But it's not going to be the most straightforward end to the season. But we'll try to do the best we can."

excerpt:
Oscar Piastri is scratching his head as to why he’s struggled to maximise the McLaren Formula 1 package compared to team-mate Lando Norris. The reigning world champion has won the last two grands prix - Budapest and Zandvoort - from pole thanks to a heavily-upgraded MCL40, while Piastri has suffered a DNF and finished sixth. It has left Norris fourth in the standings and 55 points ahead of seventh-placed Piastri, who also trails his team-mate 13-4 in their qualifying head-to-head (sprint races included) this year. Read Also:

Formula 1Who slept worst last night: Oscar Piastri

So the Australian has certainly been second best and he is without a podium since Miami in May, while his last win came at Zandvoort last August - when he looked like a champion-in-waiting. “Unfortunately it's not the first race where the pace just hasn't been there,” said Piastri on Sunday. “Lando has just won the race [by] quite a lot, so I think the car is in a good place. “It's been quick the last two weekends. I think these two tracks suit the car well. It's just for whatever reason, I've not been able to get the pace out of it.”

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

But one shouldn’t be too surprised by Piastri’s struggles in 2026, because he is now having to contend with a lower-grip car due to downforce levels reducing under the new rules. It is in low-grip conditions where the 25-year-old notoriously struggles, as Piastri’s title bid collapsed towards the end of last season at tracks like Baku, Singapore and Mexico City. So he’s had to adapt more than most and although there’s still been glimpses of his potential, like topping SQ2 and Q1 at Zandvoort, others have found that edge for when it matters. “In the driving style, there clearly must be something,” said Piastri, when asked where he lacks compared to Norris this season. “I think in qualifying this weekend I felt much more comfortable and through Q1 and Q2, okay, Q3 I didn't quite maximise it, but I was there in the fight.” The Australian qualified fourth, 0.142s off Norris and 0.040s and 0.009s behind Mercedes duo George Russell and Kimi Antonelli, respectively.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

“In the race, the story just wasn't the same at all,” added Piastri. “So, yeah, I think that's the biggest difference.” Sunday’s race saw Piastri overtake Russell at Turn 7 for third on lap three before dropping back to fourth on lap 19 due to a slow 5.4s pitstop. From then on Piastri just struggled for pace as Ferrari duo Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton also overtook him and he eventually finished 32 seconds behind Norris. When McLaren boss Andrea Stella was asked to explain Piastri’s woes, the Italian said: “I don't think it has anything to do with any psychological kind of opportunity - this is purely technical. “This weekend actually we saw Oscar expressing competitive lap times and I think in the race there were two factors that affected Oscar. “One was the fact, and this is a team responsibility, that when we pitted to cover Russell, actually we lost the position to Russell because of a slow pitstop and this is up to the team.

Oscar Piastri and Andrea Stella in Hungary Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

“Then this second stint on hard tyres, we were not able to switch these tyres on. excerpt:

"We’ve all had the statistics about the changing, younger demographic, and it’s tough out there for anybody, for any big organisation, to hold its ground given the amount of choices that are out there for the consumer. excerpt:
The past week has been a real rollercoaster for Yuki Tsunoda. Racing Bulls CEO Peter Bayer had already been informed the previous Friday of Isack Hadjar’s wrist injury and a potential driver change, but according to Tsunoda, he only received the call on Tuesday – while he was still on a beach in Greece. The Japanese driver immediately stressed that he was physically fully prepared for the stand-in appearance, although adapting to the 2026 machinery remained an important question mark. Yes, Tsunoda has extensively tested the Red Bull car – not the Racing Bulls – in the simulator this year, but the real thing is still different. Read Also:

Formula 1Yuki Tsunoda reveals beach phone call that led to surprise F1 return

But in precisely that respect, the race weekend at Zandvoort went remarkably well. Tsunoda managed to stay close to team-mate Arvid Lindblad’s lap times throughout the weekend, qualified 12th in both qualifying sessions and eventually finished the race in 11th, ahead of Lindblad. "Honestly, I think I was able to progress faster than I expected. I drove only four times out of eight months since my last race in Abu Dhabi. And with that, I did pretty well," Tsunoda said after the race. Tsunoda did acknowledge that it had been quite an adjustment going from the ground-effect cars he had become accustomed to over the previous years to the current machinery. At an energy-rich circuit like Zandvoort, energy management was not even the deciding factor, but the adjustment was still significant.

Just a few days after he was still on the beach in Greece, Tsunoda made a very good impression at the Dutch Grand Prix Photo by: Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images

"I think the most challenging part was pretty much everything – a lot of things, learning about deployment, buttons, everything, all procedures are different. And this race was also challenging because of tyre degradation, the degradation characteristic was also very different," he said. "So it was all about how to adapt to that, but honestly, the team supported me a lot. They made it easy for me to drive as fast as possible. It's a shame that I didn't score points, but I take it. I was fighting against top eight or top nine until the last few laps, I would say." "Teams have to decide if they want me or not, but they should!" The obvious follow-up question is what this means for Tsunoda’s future. Ahead of the Dutch GP, he had already indicated that F1 remains plan A, but said that he does not want to spend another year on the sidelines.

"I know what I can do and I think I pretty much showed what I can do to most of the paddock," he said. "With just one race, a couple of sessions, I was able to fight close to the points. Honestly, I think the outcome was... obviously, scoring points [would have been] better, but I think I did as much as I could." Before the opportunity with Racing Bulls arose, Tsunoda appeared to be looking primarily towards IndyCar for 2027 if no door opened in F1. But at Zandvoort, he at least showed that he can still be an asset to any midfield team under the current, complex regulations.

A full-time F1 return remains Tsunoda’s goal, although IndyCar could be an alternative. He does not want to spend another year on the sidelines Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"It's definitely better having this opportunity, rather than not having any opportunity, so not being able to show what I can do with these regulations," he said. "The rest is up to my manager and other teams who have not decided yet about next year's line-up, if they want to have me or not, but they should," laughed the man with 112 F1 starts to his name. After seven seconds, he looked up and laughed: "That’s cheeky, huh?" title: How Nico Hulkenberg avoided a massive shunt with Audi team-mate Gabriel Bortoleto
excerpt:
Audi Formula 1 driver Nico Hulkenberg says his "scary" incident with team-mate Gabriel Bortoleto was a combination of luck and judgement as the German avoided a disastrous accident in the Dutch Grand Prix. With the Zandvoort circuit still damp from a pre-race shower but dry enough for slick tyres, Max Verstappen suffered a heavy crash at the end of lap one in the final, banked corner. In reaction Bortoleto went through a 360-degree spin as his car became stationary in the middle of the track. As oncoming traffic had to take avoiding action, Bortoleto's Audi team-mate Hulkenberg was somehow narrowly able to avoid spearing into the side of the Brazilian's car, swerving around the left-hand side. "It was scary, sketchy," a relieved Hulkenberg reported. "The whole track was very dry, just that corner stayed much wetter and caught people out. It was very tricky and I wasn't sure where he was going to go, if he was going to roll up or roll down. I was waiting, hesitating until the last moment. A good portion of luck not to hit each other there, but that was too close for comfort. "I saw it happen almost in slow motion at that speed. A sheet of paper would have fit between us, but not much more." "Days of Thunder" From the pitwall, the team's racing director Allan McNish also had his heart in his mouth as he watched both onboards simultaneously. "I live every second with them, which is why I'm turning grey very quickly at times," the three-time Le Mans 24 Hours winner quipped. "Max shunted in front of him, and it was the trickiest corner on the circuit by a long way at that particular point. But it was only on the replay where it was quite evident how close it was between our two cars.

"When I first saw Gabriel spinning and then Nico coming out the other side of it, I didn't quite realise that he had gone into the smoke. So, it was a bit too much Days of Thunder for my heart..."

Allan McNish, Racing Director, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Dissecting the incident as a former racer, McNish said: "When something's happening ahead of you, there is a mental process, but there's also an instinct. In which direction? A banking is a different thing, which is why I was very impressed with what Gabi was able to do to keep it in the middle of the circuit and for it not to spoon up into the wall. "Whether it was instinct or skill and focus or anything else, I don't know. But it was a bloody good save!" title: Mercedes "hasn't got the money" to keep up with rival teams' F1 upgrades
excerpt:
Mercedes Formula 1 team principal Toto Wolff says his squad "hasn't got the money" to develop its 2026 car as much as McLaren and Ferrari are doing. Both McLaren and Ferrari have made significant progress in recent months by piling on upgrades to their respective cars, which has turned both into multiple race winners. Meanwhile, a more conservative upgrade plan at Mercedes, with little significant updates since May's Canadian Grand Prix, has eroded the Brackley squad's initial dominance. Speaking after McLaren's reigning world champion Lando Norris took his second consecutive grand prix win of 2026 in Zandvoort, Wolff said Mercedes isn't able to match what its rivals are doing in the 2026 development race. Read Also:

Formula 1Norris made his own life difficult again - but his recovery was stunning in Zandvoort's swansong

When asked by Autosport if those development decisions are now starting to become increasingly uncomfortable in light of McLaren's rapid progress, Wolff said his team's hands are tied with how it has partitioned its $215m cost cap allowance. "We haven't got the money to put developments on the car. I said before that we are trying to evenly split that through the season based on our calculations of when we can bring the biggest updates and optimising the championship points. But we just can't do what we can't do," the Austrian said. "That's why it is a development race. If you bring an upgrade, each of the top teams will have a couple of tenths in it, at least, and that's what you lose. So, yeah, the ride has been a bit tougher than at the beginning of the year."

Toto Wolff, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

When pressed on why Mercedes hasn't got the cost cap budget to bring upgrades when McLaren and Ferrari have, he replied: "You will see towards the end of the season whether they are going to be able to deploy as much stuff onto the car as they do now. "Someone might have a different strategy in spending more at the beginning and the middle of the year than towards the end." Mercedes isn't expected to bring any significant upgrades to the W17 until F1 heads overseas again, starting with the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the start of October. Wolff pointed out that the picture would have looked differently if Mercedes hadn't struggled as much with the reliability of its power unit, which has cost both Kimi Antonelli and George Russell several dozens of points thus far and will lead to grid penalties down the line. "Did we spend too much at the beginning and the initial development? I don't think so," he added. "I just think we are an organisation with a certain size and infrastructure. "In that respect we had a really quick car. We left between 50 and 100 points on the table due to reliability issues. That would have given us a little bit more of a gap than we have today. And other than that, we are just continuing to execute what the plan was and what the financial realities mean for us." Read Also:

title: Lando Norris disagrees with Kimi Antonelli and George Russell on F1's pecking order
excerpt:
Lando Norris has disagreed with Kimi Antonelli and George Russell for saying McLaren now boasts the best car in Formula 1 - arguing it’s his driving that’s making the difference. The reigning world champion has won the last two grands prix – Budapest and Zandvoort – from pole thanks to a heavily-upgraded MCL40, which went winless in the opening 10 rounds. Those early races in 2026 were dominated by Mercedes, who won the first six from pole but has only taken two victories since because of Ferrari and McLaren improving their cars. So it led to championship leader Antonelli, who finished second at Zandvoort on Sunday, saying Mercedes is “clearly” behind McLaren, and Russell agreed after finishing third in the Dutch GP. When those comments from the Mercedes duo were therefore put to Norris, he said: “Well, they’re not going to say themselves, are they? “So they’re the team to beat [even] if they just got beaten today, so I don’t think it’s true. I think if I didn’t get Kimi when I overtook him, I don’t think I would have won the race today.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

“It’s hard to say, but I also know how good of a job I’m doing behind the wheel, and of course, I’m never one to over-talk about myself, normally always the complete opposite. “But for once I would give myself a little bit of credit that I feel like I’m doing a better job than everyone, and I think that can also make a difference.” The 2026 campaign has arguably been Norris at his best because although he isn’t in the championship fight, sitting 86 points behind Antonelli, he has maximised his package.

That is evident when compared to team-mate Oscar Piastri, who finished sixth in the Netherlands to remain seventh in the standings and 55 points behind fourth-placed Norris. The Briton is also 13-4 up in their qualifying head-to-head (including sprint races) so Norris reckons it’s his driving that’s causing McLaren to look like it’s in the same league as Mercedes. He even used the Zandvoort sprint race to further illustrate his point, as Russell dominated from pole while Norris only just held off Antonelli for third – the Italian started fifth due to floor damage.

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

“We look at yesterday and in qualifying,” added the now 13-time grand prix winner, “but we didn’t win yesterday and we didn’t really change much. But I worked a lot on my driving. I want to believe more than everyone else again, and we turned things around today. “So we certainly have a very similar car, I would say, all in all, to Mercedes, but I think they have a better all-round performing car than what we do. We are more specific in high-speed [curves]. Turn 7 and Turn 8 were just our biggest two corners where I would gain time today. “But, yeah, you know, if I make one mistake in qualifying yesterday and P3, P4, P5, I’m not going to win, and then no one’s going to be saying these things. title: What Ferrari actually meant to do when Hamilton felt like a "guinea pig" in Dutch GP
excerpt:
Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur has clarified what led to Lewis Hamilton’s radio outbursts during a tough Dutch Grand Prix weekend for the Formula 1 outfit. The Scuderia finished off the podium for a second, consecutive race as Hamilton took fourth with team-mate Charles Leclerc in fifth – the reverse of Budapest – and it is clear what the defining moments were for Ferrari during Sunday’s 72-lap contest. The first occurred midway through when Hamilton had just overtaken McLaren driver Oscar Piastri for fifth and started closing in on a much slower Leclerc. But due to the tight nature of Zandvoort, the seven-time world champion found it difficult to overtake and was therefore calling for team orders which didn’t arrive, allowing Lando Norris, plus Mercedes duo Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, to increase their advantage up ahead. “Great way of wasting time guys, good job!” snapped a sarcastic Hamilton, who eventually took fourth when Leclerc made his second pitstop on lap 43 – one tour after he was initially supposed to do so. The assumption was that the Briton would come in for fresh tyres shortly afterwards, considering those around the Ferrari cars did the same, but the Scuderia opted to keep Hamilton out for much longer, which meant he eventually took the lead. But Norris and Antonelli rapidly closed in on fresher tyres, and by lap 53 they were all within a second of each other. “Are you using me as a guinea pig?” quipped Hamilton, who was practically a sitting duck as the McLaren and Mercedes respectively overtook him on laps 54 and 55. The Ferrari driver was essentially left in the dark as to why his second stint was so long - 30 laps - and it required a lap 55 virtual safety car caused by Esteban Ocon for the 41-year-old to ditch his hard tyres for a fresh set of softs.

Fred Vasseur Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

“We didn't want to tell him the strategy at this stage because we didn't want to disclose it to the competitors,” said Vasseur. “We wanted to keep him on track until the end, I think it would have been the right call. “Charles was supposed to pit. We extended one lap and it was a kind of confusion. I'm not worried about this. Everybody will be back in the briefing. They will have a clear picture about the race. “Charles was a bit frustrated at one stage about the compound. I think everybody was a bit lost about the compound. Norris started with mediums on the first start [before the red flag], then he moved to softs.

“The difference between the three compounds was very marginal today. It was difficult to have a clear picture on the strategy. Sometimes, we have to change the strategy or adapt, because we are trying to learn from the others. For them it's a bit frustrating.” So it’s obvious what dominated discussions in Hamilton’s post-race media session, during which he called for Ferrari to have ‘better execution’. He cited his former team Mercedes as inspiration, considering the late team orders the Silver Arrows quickly deployed as Russell handed second to Antonelli on lap 65 after the championship leader took softs under the VSC, while the Briton stayed out on hards. Russell initially told race engineer Marcus Dudley that “we’ve lost a double podium” as Hamilton closed in on his former team-mate, but the Mercedes driver held on for third and post-race said the swap was the correct decision.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Had it not been for the earlier fiasco with Leclerc, Hamilton reckons he’d have had a better shot at claiming a late podium and Vasseur echoed those comments, claiming “the execution today was not that good”. “You can always say after the race that it would have been better to do it on lap 46,” the Frenchman added. “The story is that, when Lewis came back on Charles, we were expecting him to pit. “Then we had someone in the shadow of the car. We asked him to do one lap more. You can't ask him to do one lap more and to swap positions in the straight line. It's not so easy. If I have a look at the race now, I can see the difference. The main issue is that we didn't tell Lewis that we were expecting him to go to the end. It was not a matter of pushing.” The result leaves Ferrari 87 points behind leader Mercedes and 75 ahead of third-placed McLaren, which has taken consecutive wins from pole via Norris, with 11 rounds remaining. title: Pierre Gasly’s warning to Racing Bulls: ‘They ruined our race, and I won’t forget it’
excerpt:
Alpine Formula 1 driver Pierre Gasly has blamed his underwhelming Dutch Grand Prix result on Racing Bulls’ team tactics in Sunday’s race, amid their tight battle in the constructors’ championship. Gasly was on form in Zandvoort, where he qualified and finished eighth in the sprint – ‘best of the rest’, in other words – although he took just 11th on the grid for the main race. A strong start, however, meant the former Racing Bulls racer swiftly climbed to eighth – but that was until his first pitstop dropped him behind Arvid Lindblad, whose drive-through penalty for a yellow-flag infringement had taken him out of contention for points. Gasly spent seven laps stuck behind Lindblad until he attempted an overtake around the outside of Turn 11, but locked up and was passed by Nico Hulkenberg, with Yuki Tsunoda now tailing him. Hulkenberg made short work of Lindblad, but Gasly still couldn’t and Tsunoda impressively overtook the Alpine into Turn 7, a move he set up in the banked Turn 3 curve. While Lindblad unsurprisingly made it easy for his Racing Bulls team-mate to go through, Gasly kept struggling. Overall, it took a whopping 17 laps in total for the Frenchman to get by.

Pierre Gasly, Alpine, behind Yuki Tsunoda, Racing Bulls Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

To compound his issues, Gasly found himself behind Tsunoda after his second pitstop and required another 10 laps to find a way past his former team-mate. “VCARB ruined our race in the middle part of the race, played a team game for the championship and did it well,” Gasly lamented. “I mean, it just made me lose a position to Nico and Tsunoda and I don't know how many seconds of race time. Congrats to them, and I can't wait to race them.”

The Racing Bulls strategy had no impact on the Faenza-based team, which failed to score points as Tsunoda and Lindblad finished 11th and 12th, but most certainly cost Gasly ninth place. He finished one second behind Fernando Alonso after losing four seconds to the Spaniard – despite new tyres – when he was behind Lindblad; then the Tsunoda stumbling block prevented the Alpine driver from catching the Aston Martin, which was one-stopping, as quickly as he could have. “It's just annoying, but it's Zandvoort,” Gasly added. “Can't really overtake, and this is going to change in the coming tracks. And good thing is I have a good memory, so I'm going to make sure we smile at the end of the year.” Yet, when Motorsport.com put Gasly’s comments to him, Lindblad was unfazed: “I don't know. Yeah, that's a nice story. In the end, yeah, I played the team game. I don’t know.

Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls Photo by: Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images

“If he has a good memory, then fine. In the end, we all fight as hard as we can every weekend. I tried to help the team where I could. The reality was, my race, I wasn't really in it anymore, so yeah, I did what I could to help the team.” The two outfits are locked in a close fight for fifth place in the constructors’ championship, with Racing Bulls on 66 points and Alpine now up to 63. title: Antonelli set for Italian GP grid penalty
excerpt:
Mercedes has officially decided its Formula 1 world championship leader Kimi Antonelli will start from the back of the grid at the upcoming Italian Grand Prix after it decided to give him a new power unit, exceeding his allowance for the year. Drivers are allowed to use up to four power units for the season, but Mercedes' reliability woes over the first half of the campaign meant it has always been a question of when, not if, its drivers were going to exceed that allowance and take a grid penalty. Antonelli is currently already at the limit with his V6 and exhaust system, while Russell has no more room for either a combustion engine or turbocharger. Antonelli had been in line for a grid drop at his home race in Monza in two weeks' time, and Mercedes has now officially confirmed it will change the title favourite's engine. The 19-year-old is set for a full power unit switch, which sets him up for a back-of-the-grid start. "With Kimi we are taking the full thing," Wolff confirmed, dismissing the notion that Mercedes could have been tempted to take into account Monza being Antonelli's home race.

Photo by: Pauline Ballet - Formula 1

"In theory, our calculations say that that's the best track to take it. Obviously, our algorithms don't take nationality into consideration. But we are here to fight for a championship and not get the most PR. So, that's what we are going to do." Russell is also set for grid drop down the line, though the Brackley team hasn't decided yet where the Briton will swap power units yet. Russell only took his fourth power unit at the recent Hungarian Grand Prix, the final race before the summer break. That gives him more flexibility on mileage, though the team could still opt to add a fifth power unit to his pool of components at any time. "With George, the discussions are ongoing about where to take it," Wolff said. The next suitable opportunity after Monza could be Baku's Azerbaijan Grand Prix, which emphasises power unit performance and top speed while providing some overtaking opportunities to offset a grid drop. title: Who slept worst last night: Oscar Piastri
excerpt:
On 31 August 2025, Oscar Piastri won the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort, while Lando Norris retired with an oil leak. Faced with that bitter disappointment, Norris said all he wanted to do was "grab a burger and go home". He was 34 points behind Piastri in the championship, and my own race report that day carried a headline asking whether Zandvoort had effectively decided the title. What a difference a year makes. Looking back now, that world almost feels like some surreal parallel universe. One in which Piastri was on the verge of becoming a Formula 1 world champion; Norris had somehow been labelled the perennial talent who, when push came to shove, could never quite get the job done; Kimi Antonelli had 64 points to George Russell's 184. I will readily admit that I, too, was among those quietly wondering whether Toto Wolff might just have got it wrong with the young Italian after all. Now, Norris is the world champion, even Nico Rosberg regards Antonelli as something akin to the next Ayrton Senna, and if the most bullish optimists genuinely believe McLaren can still have a say in the 2026 title fight, they are probably thinking of Norris alone. In the space of 12 months, Piastri has gone from champion-in-the-making to what increasingly feels like McLaren's unofficial number two. His manager Mark Webber, whom many once regarded as an important piece of the puzzle in the Australian's path to the world championship, has seemingly been reduced to a peripheral figure in Team Piastri. And with the 25-year-old finishing 32 seconds behind Norris at Zandvoort and now trailing him by 55 points in the championship, you might think that says everything. Numbers usually don't lie.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Pauline Ballet - Formula 1

It must hurt Piastri to hear Andrea Stella wax lyrical about Norris fully exploiting his exceptional talent when grip is low and tyres are hard. And then, in the same breath, explain that Piastri has to do things with the 2026 McLaren that go against his natural driving instincts simply to get anywhere near extracting the car's full potential. Not that Stella is doing anything wrong. The former Ferrari man is probably the most diplomatic team principal in Formula 1. He plays the game of words so skillfully that he would never allow even the faintest impression to emerge that he regards one of his drivers as number one and the other as number two. But a year on, plenty of those fans who have always insisted on Reddit and elsewhere that Norris was McLaren's secret favourite all along – particularly in the eyes of CEO Zak Brown – now feel vindicated. As if Norris were the first-born son, while Piastri was 'merely' the adopted child they never quite learned to love in the same way.

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Pauline Ballet / LAT Images via Getty Images

It seems unlikely that Piastri has forgotten how to race a car in the space of 12 months. But perhaps one of the reasons he lost the 2025 championship was that, after Zandvoort, the easy-going composure that might have protected him from switching from attack mode to points-management mode in response to his championship lead suddenly disappeared. And because the 2026 generation of Formula 1 cars does not appear to be the kind of toy he most enjoys playing with. "Unfortunately it's not the first race where the pace just hasn't been there," Piastri sighed after the race as he tried to explain his sixth-place finish in the TV pen. A few metres away, Norris sat all by himself in the FIA press conference, smiling and saying things like: "I'm certainly eliminating my weaknesses on track, and I don't have so many." When Piastri moved from Renault to McLaren in one of the more controversial transfers in recent Formula 1 history – a contractually convoluted cloak-and-dagger affair – he arrived with the reputation of a potential prodigy. Before reaching Formula 1, he had won (almost) everything there was to win, and after a solid, if not spectacular, rookie season alongside Norris, he spent much of 2025 appearing to justify every ounce of the hype.

While Norris spoke openly about his emotions and weaknesses – something many interpreted as a very human crack in his armour – Piastri did not say much. He simply won motor races. Cold-blooded, unflappable, stripped of unnecessary theatrics.

Race winner Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Erik Junius

But Formula 1 in 2026 has moved a long way from the version of motor racing familiar to amateur racers at indoor kart tracks, where ultimately the guy with the biggest balls wins by driving through the corners faster and cleaner than everyone else while staying out of trouble. The new Formula 1 is more like a game of chess. Having the biggest balls still matters, but intelligently juggling complex parameters such as energy deployment and extracting peak performance from the tyres has taken on overriding importance. Or, to put it another way: there was a time when being the fastest man at driving a racing car could make you world champion. In a field whose overall standard is probably higher than ever before, that alone is no longer remotely enough. It would make for a fascinating experiment to put the entire 2026 grid back into the 2025 cars. Would Piastri start winning again? Would Lewis Hamilton still struggle with the Ferrari? Ultimately, it is irrelevant. Formula 1 world championships are won in the real world. Parallel universes exist only on Reddit. And, for fans, it can be great fun to lose yourself in them. There is a difference between the Piastris of this world and the Antonellis. Antonelli burst onto the scene like a bolt of lightning in his very first Formula 1 practice session at Monza. Everyone could see that this kid was something special. A natural talent, born with the right instincts. Piastri seems more like the kind of racing driver who needs a little more time to adapt to new circumstances before he can truly flourish. That is not to suggest that he is somehow inherently less gifted. It would not surprise me in the slightest if, in a year or two, the headlines were telling a very different story again. Hamilton has proven that the genuinely great drivers should never be written off. Perhaps that is an example Piastri can cling to the next time all that overthinking keeps him awake at night... title: Who slept best last night: Liam Lawson
excerpt:
Liam Lawson's third race at Red Bull was exactly what Red Bull would have wanted from Liam Lawson. Solid qualifying, right behind Max Verstappen. No big mistakes and strong pace in the race. Points. He finally proved he deserved to be in that seat... It's just that his third race at Red Bull wasn't Suzuka in April 2025, but Zandvoort some 17 months later. So, how should we interpret Lawson's weekend? And what does it actually prove? That Lawson is a capable grand prix driver? No, not that. That's too obvious anyway. One or two races can't change that perception. Everything he's done during his career is enough. It doesn't prove he's destined to win the world championship either. One weekend is one weekend, after all. You'd need a much broader sample. It can't even be used as evidence to back the claim that he could have turned his 2025 campaign around had he been given the chance to keep driving the RB21. Because it still looks as likely as it did before this weekend that his season would have turned into a continuous nightmare, no matter what – because of the circumstances he was dealing with. Lawson was promoted to Red Bull with just 11 F1 races under his belt, spread across two short stints over two years, and thrown into a car that had been built and developed completely around Verstappen over the years.

Lawson qualified right behind Verstappen and even battled with the Dutchman on lap one Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

What Zandvoort probably proves is that the RB21 did indeed suit his driving style about as well as Esteban Ocon's overalls would fit Yuki Tsunoda – or perhaps even the other way around. With almost no experience and put under enormous pressure by bosses who seemingly only chose Lawson back then because they believed in Tsunoda even less, he was almost destined to fail – and, there's no denying it, he did so spectacularly. But it also happened at tracks he had never raced at in F1, following a difficult pre-season test, while being exposed to relentless media scrutiny fuelled by Red Bull itself. He was shown the door after failing to escape Q1 three times – including qualifying last twice on the sprint weekend in China – and inevitably scoring zero points. There was also an accident in Melbourne on a damp track, but he wasn't the only one crashing out that day, to be fair. The lack of pace, though, was just staggering. Now, in what on the face of it were even worse circumstances – with a call on Monday, a simulator session right before his departure to the Netherlands and only one free practice session to adapt to a completely new machine – Lawson's weekend was near-perfect. You can pin the blame on him for not progressing into SQ3 on Friday evening in sprint qualifying, but even Helmut Marko probably wouldn't. Lawson's gap to Verstappen in main qualifying was a tiny 0.115s, and in the race he ultimately was the only Red Bull driver to score points – and it didn't look like there was a lot more on the table for the team this weekend than his eventual P7.

You can explain it the way Verstappen did when he was asked about Lawson's qualifying performance. The Dutchman's theory suits his narrative this year: F1 2026 is so flawed that the best drivers can't make as much of a difference. Andrea Stella, who was presented with that theory a few hours later, tactfully disagreed, noting that the technology is so complex this year that tiny differences can actually result in bigger gaps. But it may well be that both are actually right. In the RB21 Lawson was handed at the start of 2025, Verstappen indeed could make a huge difference – and it didn't really matter who was driving the second car. Sergio Perez at the end of 2024 wasn't really a lot better at the wheel of the RB20. Neither was Tsunoda later.

Liam Lawson, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images

So, what did Lawson's Zandvoort weekend really prove? That Lawson can do as good a job as Isack Hadjar? No, we saw that last year. Maybe it proves that the same driver with considerably more Formula 1 experience can deal with such a challenge better? Well, that was probably fairly obvious to everyone apart from Helmut Marko and Christian Horner anyway. Maybe the only real takeaway is that Red Bull's hectic driver decisions a year and a half ago were indeed as insane as they looked back then. And that it wasn't Lawson who failed – it was those making the calls. In March 2025, explaining the decision, Helmut Marko pointed out that Red Bull wasn't simply demoting Lawson back to the junior team – it was saving his career instead. Yet his career perhaps wouldn't have needed any saving had he not been put in a position from which he had almost nothing to gain in the first place. What's bitter for Lawson in all of this is that his Zandvoort performance probably isn't going to do much for his future prospects. No, his 2027 seat isn't confirmed yet - but he was already doing a solid enough job with Racing Bulls to have a fair chance of earning another year. Will this weekend put him back in contention for the "big" Red Bull seat? Well, with Marko not around anymore, you wouldn't really expect Hadjar to get axed for no apparent reason. There's an inevitable 'what could have been' part of the story as well. Had Red Bull acted logically in the winter leading up to the 2025 season, the poisoned RB21 would probably have been Tsunoda's to take from the start. Lawson would have got another year with the Faenza squad and potentially could have started 2026 next to Verstappen – in a much friendlier car, with a lot more experience. title: George Russell "still not there" as Mercedes pressure builds after Dutch GP, says former F1 driver

title: Winners and losers from F1's chaotic Dutch Grand Prix
excerpt:
If there were any fears after Saturday's mind-numbing sprint display that the Netherlands would send off its Formula 1 revival with a dud, then those fears were washed away in a sudden shower one hour before Sunday's race, around the time the starting grid started opening for business. The rain didn't persist into the race itself, but caused just enough havoc to make Zandvoort's dune loop slippery, leading to carnage at the end of lap 1.

Photo by: Anni Graf - Formula 1 via Getty Images

Loser: Max Verstappen Of all people, it was home hero Max Verstappen who tripped up in the conditions, making a rare mistake by being too eager with his right foot coming onto the main straight. The otherwise flat-out Luyendyk corner was particularly damp, with Verstappen veering straight into the outside wall after tapping the white line on the inside. The end result was a huge crash, though the Dutchman was fortunate not to be collected by oncoming traffic. It's not the end result he or the army of orange clad fans were hoping for on the event's swansong, but both the four-time world champion and Zandvoort have had a good run, with Verstappen winning the first three editions. Verstappen's contract extension, which is supposed to keep him in F1 until 2030, should soften the blow too.

Photo by: John Thys / AFP via Getty Images

Winner: Lando Norris Saturday's sprint didn't particularly fill McLaren with confidence, with the team's inferior race pace and tyre management on the medium compound making it unable to keep up with winner George Russell, while Ferrari also looked intrinsically quicker. But in the hands of Norris, Sunday was a different story for the upgraded McLaren. While Norris was unable to hold off Antonelli on the standing restart, on Pirelli's hard tyre the reigning world champion was an absolute demon as he swept past the erstwhile leader and then picked off Lewis Hamilton on the same lap. His team boss Andrea Stella credited the team's set-up adjustments after a much poorer sprint, but also reserved special praise for Norris as Oscar Piastri struggled much more aboard the other car. "I think Lando had an extra [gear] in terms of understanding how to use this [hard] compound," Stella said. "These conditions, I think this is where he can express his natural driving style." As his most recent grand prix wins in Budapest and Zandvoort have shown, Norris is arguably operating at his peak right now.

Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

Winner: Liam Lawson Different car, different role, different team leadership. The circumstances around Liam Lawson's one-off Red Bull return couldn't have been more different than his first calamitous adventure with the squad at the start of 2025, which lasted all of two rounds. Speak to anyone who works or has worked with him, and it is clear Lawson has changed too - more mature for the character-building experience, and more well-rounded as a grand prix driver. That's all very easy to say, but in the Netherlands Lawson was actually handed a surprise opportunity to back that up with facts. Subbing for the injured Isack Hadjar, he soldiered on through his one-off weekend with aplomb, despite driving what he experienced as an "entirely different" car other than the power unit. A distant seventh-place was all that was on offer on Sunday as Red Bull was the fourth-fastest team by some distance. This is all Red Bull could have asked for from its stand-in.

Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Loser: Ferrari Yet another weekend goes by where Ferrari has a quick car but somehow manages not to bring it to the podium. Race weekend execution remains a sore topic for the Scuderia, between sub-optimal out-laps in qualifying to pitstops to race strategy. Lewis Hamilton made an astute observation on Sunday, after getting fed up with Ferrari dilly-dallying on its decision to either swap positions with Charles Leclerc or pit his team-mate, as ended up happening. When George Russell was asked to swap with Kimi Antonelli, the Briton didn't particularly like it but immediately acted, with neither driver losing much time in the process.

"Mercedes execute like that," Hamilton said. "They've got the car that's fighting for the championship in the lead, and they did it straight away. Here I'm sitting back, losing seconds. Something that we need to discuss offline." Things could have been different without the late virtual safety car, which likely saved Russell's podium spot from Hamilton. But all those little things are starting to add up as the seven-time world champion and Ferrari are trying to stay in the fight with an under-powered engine.

Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Winner: Fernando Alonso The Zandvoort weekend was shaping up to be quite bleak for Aston Martin on Friday when driveability issues with Honda's upgraded engine made it hard enough for Fernando Alonso and team-mate Lance Stroll to stay on the black stuff, never mind build on the team's Hungary progress. There still weren't any miracles on Sunday, but there was enough performance in the AMR26 to make a bold one-stop strategy work for Alonso, getting one over Alpine's Pierre Gasly and the Racing Bulls drivers. "Formula 1 is not a mysterious sport," said Alonso, the first driver aged 45 or older to score points since 1974. "You have to bring performance and outperform competitors to score points and it's what we are doing. So, congratulations everyone in Silverstone and hopefully we can bring more."

Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Loser: Williams You could make a big deal about the contact between Carlos Sainz and Alex Albon at the end of the race. But much more damning than the Williams-on-Williams violence itself is the fact that the collision, triggered by Sainz locking up his old hard tyres in Turn 1, was utterly meaningless, as the two drivers were racing nobody but themselves for 15th. Williams is stuck in survival mode until its underdeveloped package receives some much-needed upgrades in Azerbaijan. But following Aston Martin's significant step forward, it's now just racing Cadillac and - on a good day - Haas. The good news of this week is that both drivers have committed their future to the team for next year, removing some of the noise and distractions that were clouding the picture in recent weeks. But, as team principal James Vowles admitted on Friday, there won't be any short-term fixes for Williams.

Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

Winner: Yuki Tsunoda As Liam Lawson deserves praise for coming full circle on his successful Red Bull return, so does YukI Tsunoda. The Japanese driver was a spark plug on his one-off outing after spending 2026 on the sidelines, soaking it all in as he savoured an experience he wasn't sure he would ever be granted again. A future in IndyCar may well await, through Yuki Tsunoda's carefully cultivated Honda connections. But last weekend, the 26-year-old could call himself an F1 driver again, and he did a decent job sticking close to regular driver Arvid Lindblad throughout the weekend. "Honestly, I missed this kind of feeling, chasing those last few milliseconds," Tsunoda said after qualifying. "I am super enjoying it." After just missing out on a point on Sunday, he added: "I know what I can do and I think I pretty much showed what I can do to most of the paddock. "Now it's up to my manager and other teams, who haven't decided yet about next year's line-up, if they want to have me or not. Call me, please!" Tsunoda joked before being whisked away.

Photo by: Eric Le Galliot

Honourable mention: Nico Hulkenberg How can you not give Nico Hulkenberg a shout-out for his outstanding reflexes at the end of lap 1, which saved his Audi team-mate Gabriel Bortoleto from an awful accident? You can't, so fair play. Photos from Dutch GP - Sunday

title: What makes Norris say “I don't have a car to fight for the championship”?
excerpt:
The 2026 Formula 1 championship finds itself at a curious intersection where nobody is willing to entertain the idea that they have the best car. Championship leader Kimi Antonelli said after finishing second to Lando Norris in the Dutch Grand Prix that Mercedes no longer has the best car – indeed, that it may only be the third best. But Norris, now fourth in the standings with 159 points to Antonelli’s 242, was determined to play down talk of him staging a comeback in the final half of the season, despite winning two consecutive grands prix. "I don't have the car I need to fight for a championship," he said after his Dutch GP victory. Many readers would be tempted to cite the so-called Mandy Rice-Davies principle – "Well they would say that, wouldn’t they?" What’s clear, though, is that under the latest technical regulations there is still a difference in relative strengths between cars which complicates the competitive picture. In broad-brush terms the McLaren MCL40 thrives in fast corners, Ferrari’s SF-26 is strong in terms of carrying good speed into slow corners, while the Mercedes W17 is somewhere between the two. That makes the competitive balance heavily dependent on circuit layout. Norris’s contention is that his car is insufficiently rounded to be dominant across the remaining rounds in the way last year’s McLaren was the car to beat at most tracks.

Norris played down the significance of his Dutch GP victory Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"We have a strong car in certain areas," he said. "It's not like last year where we were pretty good everywhere. We're very, very strong in high speed. The place we've improved the car the most is high-speed performance. "No one matches us in high speed. And that's a good thing. My pace advantage to Mercedes in Turn 7, Turn 8 was crazy. "But their advantage that they have to us in slow speed is also crazy. And therefore I don't have the confidence to say, yeah, I can easily fight for a championship for the rest of the season. I know I've just won two races in a row and two poles in a row, but at the minute I don't have the car I need to fight for a championship. "And I know that's quite a big comment, but I think last year I understood what is needed from a car and what was needed from me. And I know the level that I am now and what I can perform at. And I know just what I need from the car – and what tracks we have coming up where we're going to certainly struggle more." The issue is more complex than simply saying a particular car is fast around a certain type of corner. This year’s cars are shorter, narrower and slightly lighter – and the chassis characteristics are more interconnected with power unit performance than ever before, given the influence of corner-entry speeds on energy harvesting.

McLaren's decision to run a short wheelbase, helping it save weight at the start of the season, has baked in certain shortcomings in terms of how much aerodynamic load the team can squeeze from the floor. Performance is often hugely variable between tyre compounds. In Saturday’s sprint race, running mediums, Norris struggled with rear degradation and was overtaken by Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc in the closing stages. In the grand prix he took the restart on used softs, was passed by Antonelli at the start, and didn’t really get into the race until the hard-compound tyres went on.

Norris was able to pressure championship leader Antonelli later in the Zandvoort race Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

"We put on the hard tyres," he said. "We were a bit more aggressive with how we wanted to approach the stint. And we turned things around. I had that feeling in the car that I wanted. I went from just not feeling like I was going to win a race to at least we can force him [Antonelli] to make mistakes. "When I get what I need from a car, when I have the front I want, when I get the confidence with the rear on entries – just when I get what I need to be able to know and predict every single corner, I'm going to win a race." Norris has a driving style slightly more aligned to Max Verstappen than the likes of George Russell or even his own team-mate, Oscar Piastri. Rather than separating the throttle off/brake on and turning phases, he likes to blend the throttle and brakes and take a shallower approach angle. Essentially he is feeling for the point in the overlap where the front tyres begin to exert more lateral grip, which helps rotate the car and carry more speed into the corner, towards the apex. This requires the car not only to have a 'strong' front end, but also to communicate what the front tyres are doing, which represents a tough engineering challenge. Modern F1 cars require a consistent ride height for the aerodynamics to function optimally, so the suspension geometry is designed to minimise dive and squat. A side of this is that it saps driver 'feel'. Some can live with that, some can’t, which is why McLaren designed an alternate front suspension geometry with a revised kingpin angle for Norris when he was floundering at the beginning of last season. Once he has that feel he can be very adaptable in terms of his lines and the degree of overlap between throttle and brake, which is why he thrives in low-grip conditions. But although he has a huge amount of adaptability within this range, he still needs that strong front end, good transmission of feel, and confidence that the rear axle will rotate predictably on cue. "It's clear where our weaknesses are," Norris concluded. "Therefore we need to attack those things. And until we do that, it's still going to be a very tough end of the season." Read Also:
